subject: physics
question_text: Define stress and explain the types of stress.

verification.note: Asked in TS March 2016 (Q17) — TS Inter I-Year Physics Paper-I, Section B, 4 marks. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: stress = restoring force per unit area, SI unit N m⁻², dimensions [ML⁻¹T⁻²]; the three types are longitudinal (tensile and compressive), volume (bulk) and shearing (tangential).

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Stress — the definition
lines: A deforming force applied to a body changes
its shape or size. The body sets up an
internal restoring force that is equal and
opposite to the applied force. Stress is this
restoring force per unit area of the surface.
SI unit: N m⁻²   Dimensions: [ML⁻¹T⁻²]
steps.margin_note: First mark. The formula alone does not earn it — the words "restoring force per unit area" must be there.
steps.why: The restoring force and the applied force are equal in size while the body stays in equilibrium, so stress can be calculated from the applied force, which is the quantity a problem gives you.
common_mistakes: Calling stress the applied force per unit area. Stress is the RESTORING force per unit area; the two are equal in size only while the body is in equilibrium.
Writing the unit as N m². The unit is N m⁻², the same unit as pressure.

recall.must_convey: That stress is the internal restoring force per unit area, sigma equals F by A, with unit newton per metre squared.
accept: unit is newton per metre squared
reject: the force acts parallel to the surface

steps.memory_tip: Stress is a force divided by an area, so it carries the unit of pressure: N m⁻².

steps.label: Longitudinal stress
lines: 1. Longitudinal stress. The force acts normal
to the cross-section, along the length of the
body, so the length changes.
It has two forms. Tensile stress stretches
the body; compressive stress shortens it.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name the type, say where the force acts, and give both of its forms.
steps.why: Longitudinal stress is the one used in Young's modulus, so naming its two forms here is what the later definition of Y rests on.
common_mistakes: Writing only tensile stress and leaving out compressive stress. Both are longitudinal.
Saying the force is tangential. In longitudinal stress the force is normal to the area.

recall.must_convey: That longitudinal stress has the force normal to the cross-section along the length, and has tensile and compressive forms.
reject: force acts on every face of the body

steps.memory_tip: Along the length: pull it and the stress is tensile, push it and the stress is compressive.

steps.label: Volume stress
lines: 2. Volume stress, also called bulk stress.
The force acts normal to every face of the
body, as when it is placed in a fluid under
pressure. The volume changes; the shape does
not.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The words "normal to every face" are what separate it from longitudinal stress.
steps.why: The force is normal in this type as well, so what marks volume stress out is that it acts on every face at once, not that it acts in a different direction.
common_mistakes: Saying the shape changes. Under a uniform pressure the volume changes and the shape stays the same.
Treating volume stress as a separate quantity from pressure. Under a fluid it is the pressure.

recall.must_convey: That volume or bulk stress acts normal to every face, as under fluid pressure, and changes the volume.

steps.memory_tip: Pressed from all sides at once: the volume changes and the shape stays the same.

steps.label: Shearing stress
lines: 3. Shearing stress, also called tangential
stress. The force acts parallel to the surface
while the opposite face is held fixed.
The shape changes; the volume does not.

lines.text: Shearing stress = F/A  (F along the surface)

steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. The word "tangential", or "parallel to the surface", is what earns it.
steps.why: Shearing stress is the one where the force lies in the surface instead of across it, and that is exactly why it changes the shape and not the volume.
common_mistakes: Confusing shear with compression. In shear the two faces slide sideways and nothing is squeezed.
Saying shear changes the volume. Shear changes the shape only.

recall.must_convey: That shearing or tangential stress has the force parallel to the surface and changes the shape, not the volume.
reject: force on every face of the body

steps.memory_tip: Shear slides one face past the other: shape changes, volume does not.

insider_note: Three of the four marks are the three types. A long definition with only two types still loses a mark.
